summary: Gives an overview of the Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) protocols and mechanisms. RSerPool offers application-independent services and protocols for building fault-tolerant and highly available client/server applications. It is informational and introduces the other documents in the suite.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5351 describes RSerPool, a set of protocols that let a client ask for a server by name rather than by address when several servers can do the same job. If the server it gets fails, the client can ask for another one, and can carry a piece of state across so the new server can pick the work up.

questions: how does rserpool find backup servers
subtitle: Reaching a group of interchangeable servers by name, and moving to another when one fails.

tldr.problem: Applications that need high availability have to hard-code a list of backup servers and handle the failover themselves, which ties the application to particular addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RSerPool gives a client a pool handle, resolves it to a list of servers through a registry, and offers two failover hooks: a signed state cookie carried to the new server and a business card naming a preferred alternative.
tldr.outcome: The protocols are described as targeted for the Experimental Track. The document is an overview; the protocol specifications are RFC 5352 and RFC 5353.

today: RFC 5351 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It is an overview of the RSerPool suite, whose protocol specifications are RFC 5352 for ASAP and RFC 5353 for ENRP, with the requirements in RFC 3237 and the threat analysis in RFC 5355.

sections.title: Introduction: The RSerPool Architecture
sections.content:
The Reliable Server Pooling protocol suite is designed to let client applications, the pool users, select a server, a pool element, from among a group of servers providing equivalent service, a pool. The protocols are currently targeted for the Experimental Track.

The architecture supports high availability and load balancing by letting a pool user identify the most appropriate server from the pool at a given time. It is built to a set of basic goals: application-independent protocol mechanisms, separation of server naming from IP addressing, use of the end-to-end principle to avoid dependencies on intermediate equipment, separation of session availability and failover functionality from the application itself, facilitation of different server selection policies, facilitation of a set of application-independent failover capabilities, and a peer-to-peer structure.

A server pool is a set of one or more servers providing the same application functionality, and the servers are called Pool Elements. Several pool elements in a pool can provide fault tolerance or load sharing. The elements register into and de-register out of the pool at an entity called the Endpoint haNdlespace Redundancy Protocol server, using the Aggregate Server Access Protocol, which is RFC 5352.

Each pool is identified by a unique byte string called the pool handle. The pool handle maps the pool to a specific pool element located by its IP address, both IPv4 and IPv6 supported, and port number, and it is what the pool user specifies when it tries to reach a server in the pool. To resolve the handle to the address needed to reach a pool element, the pool user consults an ENRP server using ASAP. The space of pool handles is assumed to be a flat space with limited operational scope, and administration of pool handles is not addressed by the RSerPool documents at this time. The protocols used between the pool user and the pool element are application-specific, and the two are assumed to be configured to support a common set of application layer protocols independent of the RSerPool mechanisms.

RSerPool gives a client several tools for migrating between servers after a failure. It lets the client identify alternative servers, either at initial discovery or in real time. It also lets the original server give the client a state cookie that can be forwarded to an alternative server to carry application-specific state, exchanged directly between the pool element and the pool user.

It is envisioned that ENRP servers provide a fully distributed and fault-tolerant registry service. They use ENRP, which is RFC 5353, to keep the pool handle mapping space synchronized. For pool users and pool elements the ENRP servers are functionally equal, so because of that synchronization either can be contacted for registration, de-registration or handle resolution.

The requirements for the framework are defined in RFC 3237. The document notes that the requirements on RSerPool in the area of load balancing partially overlap with grid computing and high-performance computing, but that the scope of both areas is completely different: grid and high-performance computing also cover managing administrative domains, data locking and synchronization, inter-session communication and resource accounting, while the intention of RSerPool is simply a lightweight realization of load distribution and session management, intended for systems with small memory and CPU resources only. Anything further is out of scope and can be provided by the application itself. The suite comprises ASAP and ENRP, a common parameter format specification in RFC 5354, a definition of server selection rules in RFC 5356, and a security threat analysis in RFC 5355.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to give a group of identical servers one name. A client asks for that name, gets back an address, and talks to it. If that server dies, the client asks again and gets another address. Nothing in the application has to know the addresses in advance, and the rule for picking which server to use lives in the protocol rather than in each application.

sections.title: The Aggregate Server Access Protocol
sections.content:
ASAP defines a set of mechanisms for creating and maintaining pools of redundant servers: registration of a new server into a pool, de-registration of an existing server, resolution of a pool handle to a server or list of servers, liveness detection for servers in a pool, and failover mechanisms for handling a server failure.

A pool comes into existence when a pool element registers the first instance of the pool name with an ENRP server, and disappears when the last element de-registers. The information needed for RSerPool, such as the address of an ENRP server to contact, is assumed to be configured into the element beforehand, and automating that configuration is not addressed at this time.

A new server joins an existing pool by sending a Registration message via ASAP to an ENRP server, giving the pool handle of the pool it wishes to join, a pool element identifier for itself chosen randomly, information about its lifetime in the pool, and what transport protocols and selection policy it supports. The ENRP server it contacts first becomes its Home ENRP server, keeps a list of its subscriptions and performs periodic audits to confirm the element is still responsive. Similar procedures apply to de-registering, or the element can simply let the lifetime it registered with expire, after which it is gracefully removed from the pool.

When an endpoint wishes to be connected to a server in the pool, it generates an ASAP Handle Resolution message and sends it to its Home ENRP server. The server resolves the handle from its knowledge of the pool's servers and returns a Handle Resolution Response via ASAP containing the IP addresses of one or more servers that can be contacted. The list may be built using server selection policies; the suite defines a few basic policies and allows external server selection input for more complex ones.

ENRP servers monitor the status of pool elements with the ASAP Endpoint Keep-Alive message, and a pool element answers with an Endpoint Keep-Alive Ack. A pool user can also tell its Home ENRP server that the element it used has become unresponsive, by sending an ASAP Endpoint Unreachable message.

For failover, the suite provides simple hooks that any application can use. Mechanisms that rely on application state or transaction status cannot be defined without knowing more about the application, but two simple ones are provided. The cookie mechanism lets the ASAP layer generate cookies that are periodically sent from the pool element to the pool user, which stores only the last one received. On failover the user sends that cookie to the new element, which gives a simple way of sharing state between elements. The old element should sign the cookie and the receiving element should verify the signature; for the pool user the cookie has no structure and is only stored and passed on. The business card mechanism lets a pool element send a business card to its peer, containing its pool handle and guidance on which other elements the peer should use for failover. That gives a pool element a way of telling the user which it considers the next best element, whether for pool considerations such as load balancing or for user considerations such as elements with the most up-to-date state information.
sections.plainLanguage: ASAP is the conversation between a client or a server and the registry. It covers joining a pool, leaving it, looking up the servers in it, checking that the servers are still there, and reporting that one has stopped answering. The two failover aids are a signed piece of state that travels with the client to the next server, and a note from one server saying which other server it would prefer to hand over to.

sections.title: The Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol
sections.content:
A set of server pools, a handlespace, is managed by ENRP servers. Pools are not valid across the whole Internet but only within smaller domains called the operational scope. The ENRP servers use the ENRP protocol to maintain a distributed, fault-tolerant, real-time registry service, and they communicate with each other for information exchange such as pool membership changes and handlespace data synchronization.

Each ENRP server initially generates a 32-bit server ID that it uses in later messaging and keeps for the lifetime of the server. It then tries to learn about the other ENRP servers in scope, either by using a pre-defined Mentor server or by sending Presence messages on a well-known multicast channel and selecting one of the responders as Mentor. A Mentor can be any peer ENRP server. The most current handlespace data is requested from the Mentor with Handle Table Requests, and the answer arrives as Handle Table Response messages that are unpacked into the local database. After that the server is ready to provide ENRP services.

Pool elements then register their presence with ASAP messages. They discover the ENRP server when it sends an ASAP Server Announce message on the well-known ASAP multicast channel. An element only has to register with one ENRP server, because the other ENRP servers supporting the pool synchronize their knowledge about pool elements using the ENRP protocol. An element may have a configured list of ENRP server addresses, in which case it sets up associations with some of them and takes the first that responds as its Home ENRP server; alternatively it can listen on the multicast channel for a set period and take the first server it hears as its Home ENRP server.

ENRP servers send ENRP Presence messages to all their peers to show liveness. Those messages also carry a checksum computed over all the pool element identities for which the sending server is the Home ENRP server. Each server keeps an up-to-date list of its peers and can compute the checksum it expects from a given peer according to its own local handlespace database. Comparing the expected sum with the sum a peer reports, a handlespace audit, detects an inconsistency, and in that case the handlespace restricted to the pool elements owned by that peer can be requested for synchronization.

If the unresponsiveness of an ENRP server is detected, the remaining ENRP servers negotiate which of them takes over the Home ENRP role for the pool elements of the failed peer. Once they reach consensus on the takeover, the server taking over sends a notification to its peers via ENRP and to the pool elements it took over via ASAP.
sections.plainLanguage: ENRP is the registry itself, and it is designed so that no single registry server is a point of failure. The servers find each other over a multicast channel, pick one as a mentor to copy the pool data from, and then keep each other honest with a checksum over the entries each one holds. If one of them stops answering, the others agree on which of them will take over the clients that were registered with it.

sections.title: Two Ways to Use RSerPool
sections.content:
In a standalone use, the application uses RSerPool to find the address of a primary server and then talks to that server directly, without further use of RSerPool services. If the initial server fails, the application uses RSerPool again to find the next server in the pool.

For a client application with an ASAP implementation available, three changes to the source code are typically required. Instead of specifying the hostnames of primary, secondary and tertiary servers, the application specifies a pool handle. Instead of using a DNS-based service such as getaddrinfo to turn a hostname into an IP address, it invokes an RSerPool service primitive provisionally named GETPRIMARYSERVER, which takes a pool handle and returns the IP address of the primary server, and the application then uses that address just as it would have used the one DNS returned. Third, failure detection and failover must be designed into each application, and when a failure is detected on the primary server, instead of translating a secondary hostname again, the application invokes a primitive provisionally named GETNEXTSERVER, which does two things at once: it tells the RSerPool layer that the server returned by an earlier call has failed, and it returns the address of the next server to contact according to the best information the layer has, such as the set of available pool elements and the pool policy in effect. At the time of the document a full API for use with the RSerPool protocols had not yet been defined.

For a server application, two changes are required. The server should invoke the REGISTER service primitive at startup to add itself to the pool with an appropriate pool handle, along with its address or mapping identifier, port and pooling policy or policies. It should invoke the DEREGISTER primitive to remove itself from the pool when shutting down. The benefits are limited compared with using all the services, but still useful: the client needs to supply a single string rather than a list of servers, the choice of server can be made dynamically by the server selection mechanism, and when failures occur they are reported to the pool through the signalling in ASAP and ENRP, so other clients eventually learn of the failure once it is confirmed elsewhere in the architecture.

With the full suite, all communication between the pool user and the pool element is mediated by the RSerPool framework, including session establishment and teardown and the sending and receiving of data, so the application must use the RSerPool service primitives rather than the transport layer primitives of TCP, SCTP or whatever it was using. Sessions rather than connections are established, and the destination is a pool handle rather than a list of addresses with a port number. Failover from one pool element to another is then fully automatic and can be transparent to the application, as long as the application saved enough state in a state cookie.

The framework's control channel keeps the pool element lists and policies current. Because the application data is managed by the framework, unsent data, meaning data not yet submitted to the underlying transport protocol, is automatically redirected to the newly selected pool element on failover, and if the transport supports retrieval of unsent data, as SCTP does, that data can be re-sent too. A pool element can provide a state cookie that the ASAP layer at the pool user automatically passes to another pool element on failover, so the new element can recreate the state needed to continue an interrupted session or transaction. The application client can also provide a callback function invoked on the pool user side on failover, which can generate the messages that help the new pool element construct the state needed to continue an in-process session. If pool user A is also a pool element in pool X, it can pass a business card to pool element B identifying it as a member of pool X, so that if A fails, or the link between them fails, B can use the card to contact an equivalent element from pool X. If the application at A knows which elements of pool X it would prefer B to contact, it can provide that list to the ASAP layer, and it will be included in A's business card.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two levels of use. A minimal one keeps the application talking to the server itself and only asks RSerPool for an address, so the application must detect the failure and ask for another address. The full one hands the whole session over to the framework, which then moves unsent data to the new server, passes along the state cookie, and can call back into the application to rebuild whatever it needs.

sections.title: Security, IANA and Implementation Notes
sections.content: The document identifies no security requirements beyond those already documented in the ENRP and ASAP protocol specifications, and a security threat analysis of RSerPool is provided in RFC 5355. It requires no additional IANA actions beyond those already identified in the ENRP and ASAP protocol specifications. A reference implementation of RSerPool is available, described in a doctoral thesis on the architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is required here. The security rules live in the two protocol specifications and in the separate threat analysis, and a reference implementation exists.

viz.caption: THE FIVE MECHANISMS DEFINED BY ASAP

items.title: Registration
items.text: A server joins a pool by sending a Registration message with the pool handle and its own identifier.

items.title: De-registration
items.text: A server leaves the pool, or is removed gracefully when the lifetime it registered with expires.

items.title: Handle resolution
items.text: A Handle Resolution message returns the IP addresses of one or more servers in the pool.

items.title: Liveness detection
items.text: Endpoint Keep-Alive messages and their acknowledgements, plus an Endpoint Unreachable report from a user.

items.title: Failover
items.text: The cookie mechanism for carrying state, and the business card mechanism for naming a preferred alternative.
